L59: 
L60: For integers $k\geq 3$ and $D,n\geq 1$, a $k$-sunflower in $[D]^{n}$ is a collection of $k$ pairwise distinct vectors $\mathbf{x}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{k-1}\in[D]^{n}$ such that, in each coordinate, their entries are either all equal or pairwise distinct. Let $V_{k}(D,n)$ be the maximum size of a subset of $[D]^{n}$ containing no $k$-sunflower.
L61: For the reduction to the set problem, it suffices to find one fixed alphabet size $D$ and a constant $1\leq C<D$ such that $V_{k}(D,n)\leq C^{n}$ for every $n\geq 1$. In Section 【11†4】, we prove this implication for arbitrary $k$ using a probabilistic refinement of the block construction underlying the reduction of Naslund and Sawin. We average over random block choices within each family of sets of a fixed size, and then sum the resulting bounds over the possible sizes.
L62: This gives the quantitative saving needed for Theorem 【54†1】.
L63: For all integer $D\geq 3$, Naslund and Sawin [【35†44】, Theorem 2] proved
L64: 
L65:  | $$V_{3}(D,n)\leq\left(\frac{3(D-1)^{2/3}}{2^{2/3}}\right)^{n},$$  |

L67: which establishes the power-saving upper bound for the case $k=3$ of the vector sunflower problem.
L68: Their proof uses a Fourier character expansion of a symmetric function that is nonzero precisely when its three entries are all equal or pairwise distinct. Each term in this expansion has a constant factor in at least one of the three variables. After multiplying across coordinates, some vector therefore contributes at most $2n/3$ nontrivial characters, and counting these character products gives the exponent $2/3$ of the alphabet size in their bound.
L69: Our main new ingredient is an interpolation construction of a local function for arbitrary $k$. We choose its nonzero values on all-distinct tuples to depend on the entries, and use successive interpolation to arrange that every term has a polynomial factor of degree at most $k-2$ in one of the last $k-1$ variables, with the remaining factor independent of that variable. These low-degree factors all lie in a common space of dimension $k-1$.
L70: After multiplying across coordinates, a pigeonhole argument and a count of the resulting polynomial factors give the exponent $1-1/(k-1)$ below.
L71: ###### Theorem 2.
L72: 
L73: Let $k\geq 3$ and $D,n\geq 1$ be integers. Then
L74: 
L75:  | $$V_{k}(D,n)\leq\bigl(C_{k}\cdot D^{1-1/(k-1)}\bigr)^{n},$$  |
L76: 
L77: where $C_{k}=(2k)^{2/(k-1)}$.
L78: 
L79: The saving in the power of $D$ is crucial in the reduction step. In particular, taking $D=16k^{2}$ gives $C_{k}D^{1-1/(k-1)}<D$, and the reduction in Section 【11†4】 then yields Theorem 【54†1】. We now describe the main ideas behind the vector bound.
L80: We aim to bound the size of a sunflower-free family in $[D]^{n}$ by constructing a function of $k$ vectors from $[D]^{n}$ with two properties. On the family, it should equal $1$ when all input vectors coincide and vanish otherwise. It should also admit an expansion in which every term has a factor from a small common polynomial space in one of the last $k-1$ vectors, multiplied by a function independent of that vector.
L81: An elementary linear-algebra argument will then bound the size of the family by the dimension of this space.
L82: To obtain the first property, we exploit the fact that the sunflower condition can be checked separately in each coordinate. We define a local function that equals $1$ when all entries are equal, is nonzero when they are pairwise distinct, and vanishes otherwise. Multiplying this function across coordinates gives the required values on a sunflower-free family. The challenge is to obtain the second property as well. Here we use the freedom to choose the nonzero values on all-distinct tuples.
L83: Successive interpolation will construct these values so that the resulting function has an expansion with the required low-degree factors.
L84: To do this, we start with the product of the indicators that each entry equals the first, and replace its factors one at a time by interpolation polynomials. The interpolation makes the remaining error vanish as soon as an entry repeats an earlier one. At the end, the error is therefore nonzero precisely on all-distinct tuples. Subtracting it gives the desired local function, together with an expansion in which each term has a factor of degree at most $k-2$ in one of the last $k-1$ variables.
L85: We then multiply across coordinates and expand into monomials. The pigeonhole principle ensures that each monomial has low exponents in at least $\lceil n/(k-1)\rceil$ coordinates of some vector. Grouping terms according to such a vector gives the required decomposition with a common polynomial space. Counting the monomials spanning this space yields Theorem 【55†2】.

L303: ## 5 Concluding remarks
L304: 
L305: In this paper, we settle the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture by showing that any $k$-sunflower-free family of subsets of $[n]$ is exponentially smaller than the total number of subsets $2^{n}$.
L306: The closest sibling of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture is the Erdős-Rado sunflower conjecture [【21†20】], which trades the dependency on the size of the ground set for the dependency on the maximum size of the sets. More precisely, they conjectured that for any fixed $k$, any collection of sets of size at most $r$ that does not contain a $k$-sunflower has size at most $c_{k}^{r}$ for some constant $c_{k}>1$.
L307: The current record towards this problem is $O(k\log r)^{r}$, coming from a breakthrough paper by Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang [【40†4】], with subsequent refinements by Rao [【20†49】] (Tao [【64†54】] found a different proof of this result using Shannon entropy) and Bell, Chueluecha and Warnke [【50†6】]. It was mentioned, already in 1971, in [【23†25】], that the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture implies the Erdős-Szemerédi one.
L308: The implication in the other direction remains open, although Alon, Shpilka, and Umans [【16†2】] showed that if one can show an exponential upper bound in the vector variant of the problem (namely $V_{k}(D,n)$) which is independent of the alphabet size $D$, then one would prove the Erdős-Rado Conjecture. Our bounds, while yielding a polynomial saving in alphabet size, remain heavily alphabet-dependent.
L309: We made no particular efforts to optimize the base of the exponent in our bounds and have opted instead to focus on making the argument as approachable as possible. For example, we are using a coarse version of the multiplicative Chernoff bound in our proof of 【55†Theorem 2】, and are very wasteful in our estimates around that argument.
L310: There are several further optimizations readily available, such as, for example, noticing that in the proof of 【55†Theorem 2】 we put every low-degree factor in the common space $\operatorname{span}\{1,t,\ldots,t^{k-2}\}$, whereas the factor selected at stage $j$ belongs to $U_{j}=\operatorname{span}\{1,t,\ldots,t^{j-1}\}$, which has dimension $j$. With a bit more work, one can exploit this observation to improve the base of the exponent in the upper bound on the vector sunflower problem slightly.
L311: We note that this still falls short of improving the best-known base in the $k=3$ case in the set family problem, due to Naslund and Sawin [【35†44】]. We note that in the vector sunflower problem on $[D]^{n}$, for $k=3$ our argument does improve the $O(D^{2/3})^{n}$ bound from [【35†44】] to $O(\sqrt{D})^{n}$. This also translates to a similar minor improvement in the restricted-union variant of the uniform Erdős-Rado setting via the reduction of Hegedűs [【37†34】].
L312: ### 5.1 Applications, connections and limitations
L313: The new bound on the vector sunflower problem of Alon, Shpilka and Umans [【16†2】] (【55†Theorem 2】) extends to indexed multicolored sunflowers [【16†2】, 【35†44】] and limits the hard instances supplied by the vector-based reduction for arithmetic property testing in [【65†33】, Theorem 3.3]. The set system bound (【54†Theorem 1】) gives consequences for equal subset sums [【16†2】] and harmonic least-common-multiple patterns [【45†52】, 【47†42】], which we explain in a bit more detail below.
L314: Further consequences concern biased measures and weighted families [【47†42】], and the density of sunflower-free families of subspaces [【66†36】, 【67†46】]. The polynomial argument also connects to cap sets and tricolored sum-free sets [【52†19】, 【18†7】], while the set bound gives alternative exponential estimates for weak $\Delta$-systems, equidistant sets and odd sunflowers with an odd number of members [【42†45】, 【43†31】].
